6. The parties adduced oral and documentary evidence in support of their respective claims. On behalf of the plaintiff P.W. 1 Hemanta Kumar Biswas, a surveyor of the Collectorate was examined. P.W. 2 is Haji Amjed Ali Mridha who has a. shop outside the suit land. P.W. 3 Golam Mohiuddin is an Aratdar having his gaddi Oar about 20/25 cubits from the suit land. P.W. 4 is Khadem Ali Sikdar, a Touzi Nabish and a Revenue Peshkar. He was also a jama Nabish in the State Acquisition Department. P.W. 5 is a clerk of S.A. Department, record room. In addition to the oral evidence, a large number of documents were also proved and marked exhibits in the suit. These are Exhibit No. 1 sketch map showing the foreshore land of the river Barisal in mouza Amanatganj. It was prepared by P.W. 1 H.K. Biswas on .13.1.53. This document was however admitted on objection by contesting defendants. Exhibit No. 2 is the original register VI. Exhibit No. 3 is certified copy of order sheet of Miscellaneous Case No. 167' of 1957 containing the order of the Settlement Officer. Exhibit 3A is the certified copy of order in Miscellaneous case No. 1 of 1958 by the Director of Land Records. Exhibit 4 is the order of A.O. Raziur Rahman, District Magistrate dated 22.2.56. Exhibit 5 is the petition dated 13.2.57 in Miscellaneous Case No. 167 of 1957. Exhibit 1(a) is a map of mouza Amanatganj. Exhibit 1(b) is another sketch map of the disputed land prepared by M. K. Biswas P.W.1. This map was admitted in evidence with objection of the contesting defendants. Exhibit 1(c) is the certified copy of Thak map. This was also admitted in evidence with objection. Exhibit 6 is the Written statement filed by Syed Hatem Ali in Misc. case No. 67 of 1957. Exhibit 7 is the S. A. Khatian No. 217 of mouza Amanatganj. Exhibit (d) is another sketch map. Exhibits 3(b) and 3(d) are two orders in Misc. case No. 4 of 1954-55 in S.A. proceedings. Exhibits 8, 8(a) and' 8(b) are certain petitions.  13. In order to appreciate the contentions raised by the learned Advocates, it is necessary to go into the genesis of the claim. We are' not oblivious as to the changes in the topographical position of the suit land during a period of about a century. We shall refer to such positions at the proper time. It is evident from the plaint that the plaintiff laid foundation for the claim on two-fold basis. One is that the suit land is a foreshore land of river Barisal known as Kirtonkhola and the same appertains to mouza Char Badna. The clear language and the expressions used in the plaint indicates that the plaintiff was sure as to the nature of suit land as foreshore land of river Kirtonkhola appertain to mouza Char Badna. Mr. Pal has also laid considerable emphasis on this part of the plaintiff's claim. There is no dispute that river Kirtonkhola lies to the contiguous east of the present suit land. We have been addressed by the learned Additional Attorney General relating to the topographical developments occurring from the time of Thak survey which was held in 1960 when the suit land was a part of mouza Amanatganj within the Thak line. In 1867-68 the revenue survey indicated some portion of mouza Amanatganj was diluviated and the plaintiff claimed that the river Kirtonkhola shifted its course to the west and diluviated certain areas reducing the total area of mouza Amanatganj. This is evident from the C. S. map of 190 P-2. In the C. S. map, however, the land of Char Badna was recorded in zero khatian and a portion of Amanatganj contiguous to the west of the river Kirtonkhola was recorded in plot No. 829. According to the learned Additional Attorney General, mouza Char Badna belonged to the Government in proprietary right including the river and its bed. There is nothing on record to indicate with the diluvion of certain portion of mouza Amanatganj the interest of the proprietors in the Tauzin were in any way affected. There is no evidence to show that the revenue of the touzi of the proprietors relating to mouza Amanatganj was reduced because of the dilution. One sided claim of the Government extending the limits of Char Badna mouza did not extinguish the lawful interest of the proprietors of the Taluk and, therefore, the proprietary interest of Bauphal Estate remained unaffected notwithstanding the diluvion of some land of mouza Amanatganj. During R. S. operation extending a period from 1941 to 1945 and thereafter in 1952, there was a notification as claimed by the plaintiff on 26.12.52 to swallow up the diluviated portion of mouza Amanatganj within the boundary of mouza Char Badna. In our opinion, this representation indicates that the suit land was not recorded in the R.S. operation as claimed by the plaintiff. In S.A. operation also, according to the evidence of P.W. 1, the suit land was not depicted as diluviated. The defence case, on the other hand, is that the process of diluviation started from 1935 with gradual reformation in situ around 1940 and the diluviated land of mouza Amanatganj belonging to the Bhuphal Estate reappeared in situ. The landlords took possession and thereafter granted settlement in terms of Amaldari at a rental of Rs. 88/- pepper year. The defence further case is that the settlement holders came in possession of the land which was partly fit fir cultivation and partly in the process of being fit. They did cultivation for certain years in some parts and when the soil became hard and fit for raising construction they made some constructions and had been continuing in possession till their structures were forcibly demolished pursuant to a notice under Act X of 1953. The High Court in a Writ petition at the instance of Syed Hatein Ali found possession of defendant No. 1 on the basis of some title and accordingly held that the possession was not unauthorized and that the defendants were not liable to be evicted in terms of 'the notice under Act X of 1.953. The High Court also noticed the respective contentions on the conflicting title. Considering these facts in the light of the pleading and the evidence, we may quoted here paragraph 29 of the plaint to indicate the plaintiff's basis of title as disclosed in the plaint. Paragraph 29 of the plaint runs as follows:- 

 "That Mouza Amanatganj and Mouza Char Badna are different and separate neighbouring mouzas, that during the C.S. operations of the year 1903-04, Mouza Amanatganj extended upto the western bank of the Kirtonkhola navigable river and the entire Kirtonkhola river fell in mouza Char Badna and this river Kirton khola was recorded in mouza Char Badna zero khatian during C.S. operation. The bed of the Kirton khola river belonged to Government. So lands formed out of the bed of the river Kirtonkhola are pure and simple Government lands in mouza Char Badna. The Chowdhyarashi Zaminders can have no claim of any right, title and interest in these newly formed lands of mouza Char Badna. The Chowdhyarashi Zaminders could not also therefore grant any lease of any land in mouza Char Badna."
